analysis.one_liner: Cuts capital gains taxes, expands IRAs, caps federal spending growth, and adds cost reviews for new regulations.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in any committee and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cut the tax rate on capital gains to 15% (7.5% for lower-income investors), indexed asset values to inflation so gains from inflation aren't taxed, restored and expanded IRA deductions, capped federal spending growth at 2% a year through 1998, and required economic cost analysis of new federal regulations. It was referred to four House committees, sent to subcommittees, and never taken up. It died when the 103rd Congress ended without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors and corporations would gain the most, from the 15% capital gains rate, inflation-indexed asset basis, and faster depreciation write-offs. Middle-class savers would also benefit from restored, larger IRA deductions and penalty-free withdrawals for first homes, college, or catastrophic medical bills. Businesses would gain from lighter regulatory analysis requirements.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the individual and corporate capital gains tax rate to 15%, with a 7.5% rate for low- and middle-income taxpayers, and indexes the basis of stocks and business assets to inflation so gains caused by inflation are not taxed.

Restores the IRA deduction for workers covered by employer plans, doubles the maximum IRA deduction to $4,000, and allows penalty-free early withdrawals for a first home, college costs, or severe medical expenses.
Caps growth in federal spending at 2% per year through fiscal 1998 and directs House committees to produce legislation cutting spending to reach those levels.
Requires cost analyses of new regulations and extends a moratorium on new federal rules, aiming to reduce compliance costs for businesses.

analysis.who_pays: Federal revenues would fall from lower capital gains taxes and accelerated depreciation, so either deficits rise or other spending is cut. The 2% spending cap would force cuts spread across federal programs, which would fall on whoever relies on them — particularly the caps' effect on programs for low- and middle-income households.

drawbacks.text: Cutting the capital gains rate to 15% directs the largest tax savings to households with the biggest investment gains, since most stock wealth is concentrated at the top; a typical household with no taxable investments gets nothing from this provision.

The 2% cap on federal spending growth through 1998 would have forced cuts relative to what program costs would otherwise be, hitting domestic programs that working families rely on, all to make room for lower capital gains taxes.

Reduced taxes on capital gains and inflation-indexed depreciation mean less federal revenue, which the bill pairs with lower projected deficits only by assuming large spending reductions — an honest supporter would acknowledge the tax cuts would widen deficits unless matched by program cuts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's centerpiece — cutting the capital gains rate to 15% and indexing gains to inflation — would deliver the large majority of its tax benefit to households that own most corporate stock, while adding to the deficit. Restoring the IRA deduction and allowing penalty-free withdrawals for a first home or college would have helped middle-class savers. The 2% spending cap would have forced cuts across programs working families rely on to shrink the deficit largely created by those same tax cuts. Weighed honestly, the tax cuts dominate the bill, and their benefits and costs land on very different people.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four committees, bounced between two subcommittees, and never came up for a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced by Rep. David Dreier on April 28, 1993, the bill was referred jointly to the Ways and Means, Budget, Judiciary, and Government Operations committees.
In May and August 1993 it was referred to subcommittees in two of those committees, but no committee or subcommittee ever reported it.
No further action was taken before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, and the bill never received a vote in the House or Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Capital gains tax rates stayed at existing levels and federal spending was not capped, so the bill's tax and spending changes never took effect. Because it died with no debate or vote, no committee ever weighed its provisions on the merits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one — the bill simply died in committee

for.name: Rep. David Dreier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor in April, May, and August 1993.

for.name: 22 House Republicans (cosponsors)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Republicans, in a House where Democrats held the majority and controlled which bills moved, and the bill died in committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Investors and holders of corporate stock
industries.note: A 15% capital gains rate plus inflation indexing would cut taxes on gains from stock and business assets, which are disproportionately held by the wealthiest households.

Inflation-adjusted depreciation deductions, a regulatory cost-analysis requirement, and a moratorium on new rules would reduce compliance and tax costs for companies; those savings come with reduced federal revenue and weaker new regulations.

industries.industry: Financial services and retirement plan industry
industries.note: Larger, universally deductible IRAs would channel more household savings through IRA accounts held by banks and investment firms, while penalty-free withdrawals for homes, education, and medical expenses would let savers use their own money more flexibly.
